deep.reconstruction:
This page holds no mathematics. It is the title or wrapper sheet (Umschlag) of a bundle of working papers. In Gauss's hand it reads: 'Rechnungen die Lemniscatischen ſſ betreffend. (vornämlich solche, bei denen von meinen Methoden die Factoren grosser Zahlen zu finden und von den Wolframschen Logarithmentafeln Gebrauch gemacht wird)'. In English: 'Computations concerning the lemniscatic ſſ (chiefly those in which use is made of my methods for finding the factors of large numbers and of Wolfram's tables of logarithms).' Below, in pencil and a different, later (archival) hand: '51 Bl[ätter] + Umschl.-Bl.', i.e. 51 leaves plus the wrapper leaf.

Interpretation (mine, not on the page):
- 'ſſ' is Gauss's abbreviation for the lemniscatic functions or integrals: sl, cl, the integral ∫dx/√(1−x^4), and the constant ϖ.
- The bundle presumably holds high-precision numerical work: values of ϖ, the arithmetic-geometric mean M(1,√2), and lemniscatic function values and their logarithms.
- Isaak Wolfram's 48-decimal tables of natural ('hyperbolic') logarithms appear in Vega's Thesaurus Logarithmorum Completus (1794). They cover the integers up to about 2200 and the primes up to about 10009.
- A standard way to get the natural log of a large argument to many decimals is to write it as a nearby integer that factors completely over the tabulated primes, times a small correction handled by series.
- That technique explains why Gauss's factorization methods are paired with Wolfram's table. His methods are the exclusion method with quadratic residues and quadratic forms, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 329–334.
- Integer factorization may also bear on the arithmetic of lemniscate division (primes p ≡ 1 mod 4). This is speculative.

results.what: Description of a bundle of high-precision numerical computations on the lemniscatic functions, using factorization of large integers together with Wolfram's 48-place natural-logarithm table
results.modern_name: High-precision computation of the lemniscate constant / lemniscatic function values via log tables and factorization
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (lemniscatic computations, c. 1797–1800, published in Werke III/X)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a cover sheet describing the contents. Gauss's extensive lemniscatic numerics, his factorization methods and his use of Vega/Wolfram tables are all well documented. The only small point of interest is his explicit statement that he combined factoring with Wolfram's tables in these computations.
